title: Calcium isotopes link ocean acidification to Aptian-Albian foraminiferal extinctions.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC says this paper is not open access and has no PubMed Central copy, no supplementary files, no accessions and no database cross-references. I searched Zenodo (0 hits for the article identifier and 0 for the topic), Dryad (0 hits), Figshare (API unreachable), PANGAEA and the EarthChem Library (no matching deposit found). Every science.org URL I tried (article page, two guessed supplement paths) returned HTTP 403, so no data file was opened.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the measurements comes from the abstract plus the Northwestern University and EurekAlert press releases: calcium isotope ratios (the ratio of two calcium atom types, written delta-44/40-Ca) measured on planktic (open-water) foraminifera, benthic (sea-floor) foraminifera, bulk carbonate and authigenic (in-sediment) calcite from one Deep Sea Drilling Project core on the Falkland Plateau (Site 511), plus shell size, diversity and thickness counts. No sample count, no table, no units column was ever seen.

a1_downloadable.note: The article and its supplementary data tables sit behind science.org, which returns HTTP 403 to any non-browser request, and the project rules forbid scraping publisher sites. No mirror copy exists: Zenodo, Dryad, PANGAEA and the EarthChem Library all returned nothing for this study, and Europe PMC records no accession or database link. No data file could be retrieved.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no prediction target column. The quantity of interest (biological calcification rate, or extinction severity) is not measured; it is inferred by the authors from the isotope curve using a geochemical mass-balance argument, so any machine-learning label would have to be constructed by the modeller.

a3_inputs_present.note: Could not be checked, because no file was retrieved. From the paper text the inputs would be a handful of geochemical columns per core depth, not a feature set.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are conventional and unambiguous for this field (per mil relative to a standard for delta-44/40-Ca, metres below sea floor for depth, micrometres for shell size), but this rests on the paper's description, not on an opened file.

a5_enough_rows.note: A single-core stratigraphic isotope record. The press release describes 'hundreds of fossilized specimens', but individual picked shells are pooled into one measurement per depth level per material type, so the labelled unit count is realistically tens to low hundreds of rows, far under the 1,500-row bar (or 400 for classification). No exact count was verifiable because the supplement is unreachable.

a6_fits_laptop.note: A few spreadsheet tables. Size is never the problem here; the problem is that there is almost nothing to load.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be assessed: the paper states no sample count in its abstract, and no download exists to compare against.

a8_label_provenance.note: The isotope measurements are real mass-spectrometer values, but the thing one would want to predict (calcification rate) is derived from those same isotope values through the authors' model, so a model predicting it from the isotopes would be learning their equation, not biology. That is leakage by construction, the second failure mode under A8.

honest_claim_h3: No honest machine-learning claim is available: with tens to low hundreds of depth-indexed measurements from one drill core, any model would be describing a single time series rather than learning a transferable relationship.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use calcium isotope and shell-shape measurements down one drill core to predict ancient plankton calcification collapse.
plain_idea.train_on: Per-depth geochemical measurements from Deep Sea Drilling Project Site 511 on the Falkland Plateau: calcium isotope ratios for open-water foraminifera, sea-floor foraminifera, bulk carbonate and in-sediment calcite, alongside shell size, thickness and species-diversity counts. Number of rows: unknown, and probably only tens to low hundreds.
plain_idea.predict: Calcification rate, or extinction severity, at each depth. The true answer is not measured anywhere: the authors infer it from the same isotope values using a geochemical mass balance, so there is no independent ground truth.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Paleoceanographers care a lot about whether isotope excursions can be read as calcification signals, but at this sample size the question is answered by a cross-plot, not a model; the main thing learned would be that the dataset is too small to support machine learning.

ml_idea: The only project this data supports is a regression or classification of inferred calcification rate from calcium isotope ratios and shell measurements along a single Cretaceous drill core. It dies three times over: the data cannot be downloaded without the publisher's paywalled site, the sample count is a stratigraphic series of tens to low hundreds rather than thousands of independent rows, and the target would be derived from the same isotope values used as features. A viable version of this idea would need a compiled, multi-site calcium isotope database (hundreds of cores) joined to independent calcification or shell-weight measurements from culture experiments, which this paper does not provide.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the entire dataset is a small set of spreadsheet tables of stratigraphic measurements, so compute is irrelevant to the decision.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in the supplementary data table. Any single-core isotope stratigraphy will have well under 1,500 labelled depths, which kills it on A5 before any download problem matters.

verdict_reason: Paywalled with no repository copy anywhere (A1), a single drill core giving tens to low hundreds of measurements instead of thousands of rows (A5), and a target that is inferred from the very isotope values that would be the features (A2 and A8). Excellent geoscience, not a machine-learning dataset.
